tip: Welsh has no verb for have; it uses ‘gyda’ (with): ‘tocyn sbâr gyda ti’ = literally a spare ticket with you.
In a negative, ‘erioed’ means never in all past time: ‘dyw e erioed wedi bod’ = he has never been.
Reported clauses use ‘bod’, softened to ‘fod’, for that: ‘cyfaddefodd e fod e wedi gwneud’ = he admitted that he had made.
‘cwrdd’ takes ‘â’ to mean meet with: ‘cwrdd â chi’ = meet you, where ‘â’ here is with.
The word ‘i’ (to) softens the next word: ‘i Ddulyn’ (from ‘Dulyn’) = to Dublin.
A feminine noun softens its adjective: ‘awyr’ is feminine, so ‘glas’ becomes ‘las’: ‘awyr las’ = blue sky.
The ‘-wyd’ ending marks a passive with no doer named: ‘gwrthodwyd y pryd’ = the meal was sent back.
‘o'r blaen’ means before now and pairs with ‘wedi’ (have): ‘wedi bod yma o'r blaen’ = have been here before.
‘nag’ means than before a vowel (‘na’ before a consonant): ‘yn fwynach nag arfer’ = milder than usual.
‘eisoes’ means already and sits just before ‘wedi’: ‘mae e eisoes wedi pacio’ = he has already packed.
‘heb’ is the not-done counterpart of ‘wedi’: ‘heb symud’ = not having moved, where ‘wedi symud’ would mean having moved.
‘erbyn’ marks a deadline, not a moment: ‘erbyn wyth o'r gloch’ = by eight o'clock, meaning done before then.
The word ‘yn’ (in) becomes ‘yng’ and nasal-changes a place name: ‘Ceredigion’ turns into ‘yng Ngheredigion’.
The ‘-odd’ ending is the he/she past for one finished event: ‘methodd’ = he failed, ‘pasiodd’ = he passed.
‘mynd i'r afael â’ is a fixed phrase for tackling a task, and the ‘â’ on the end literally means with.
Aches and pains take ‘ar’ (on), not a verb for have: ‘arna i’ means on me, so ‘cur pen arna i’ is a headache on me.
‘dy’ (your) softens the next word, so ‘pen’ (head) becomes ‘ben’ in ‘dy ben’.
‘pont’ (bridge) is feminine, so it softens to ‘bont’ after the article ‘r’: ‘mae'r bont’.
After a number the noun stays singular: ‘deuddeg mis’ is twelve month, not months.
‘ein’ (our) adds an h before a vowel, so ‘iechyd’ (health) becomes ‘hiechyd’ in ‘ein hiechyd’.
‘neu’ (or) softens the next word, so ‘pensil’ becomes ‘bensil’ in ‘neu bensil’.
‘gan fod’ means because or since: it combines ‘gan’ with ‘fod’, a form of ‘bod’ (to be).
The ‘-wyd’ ending makes a passive, so ‘paratowyd’ means was prepared, and the doer follows ‘gan’ (by): ‘gan y plant’.
Welsh has no verb for have: ‘mae gen i’ is literally there is with me, so ‘mae gen i ewythr’ is I have an uncle.
‘heb’ (without) softens the next word, so ‘gwybod’ (to know) becomes ‘wybod’ in ‘heb wybod’.
‘cystal â’ means as good as, and ‘â’ changes ‘cawl’ to ‘chawl’, turning c into ch.
‘edrychwn ymlaen at’ is the set phrase for look forward to: it takes ‘at’, not ‘i’, before what you await.
‘a’ (and) changes the next word, so ‘cig’ (meat) becomes ‘chig’ in ‘a chig moch’, turning c into ch.
Welsh has no verb for have: possession is shown with ‘gyda’, so ‘awgrymiadau gyda ti’ literally means suggestions with you.
To report knew that, Welsh uses ‘fod’ plus the person: ‘gwyddwn i fod e'n dod’ means I knew that he was coming.
